title: Curriculum

html:
The formal definition of intrinsic motivation as the time-derivative of description length (rtint=−∂Lt/∂tr_t^{\text{int}} = -\partial L_t / \partial t) offers a normative explanation for the structured developmental trajectories observed in biological agents. If an agent is driven to maximize the rate of compression, it will naturally gravitate toward stimuli of intermediate complexity–the so-called "Goldilocks Zone" 1, 2, 3 or "Zone of Proximal Development" 4. This preference is not a heuristic but an optimality condition relative to the agent’s current model class, priors, and capacity: totally predictable stimuli yield no new compression (LtL_t is already minimal), while chaotic or wholly alien stimuli yield no progress (LtL_t cannot be reduced). Thus, the agent’s attention is sequestered in the narrow band of the "learnable," where ΔL\Delta L is maximized. The looking-time result illustrates the proposed learning-progress frontier (Figure). The macaque result extends the attention–surprise comparison across species (Figure).

Formally, let ΔL(π,θt)\Delta L(\pi, \theta_t) denote the expected description-length reduction from following policy π\pi given current model parameters θt\theta_t, and let C(π)C(\pi) denote the cost (time, energy, risk, opportunity cost). The optimal curriculum policy maximizes compression rate per unit cost:

π*=arg⁡maxπΔL(π;θt)C(π),\pi^* = \arg\max_\pi \frac{\Delta L(\pi; \theta_t)}{C(\pi)}, where C(π)C(\pi) aggregates time, metabolic expenditure, and opportunity costs. The Goldilocks zone emerges because 𝔼[ΔL]\mathbb{E}[\Delta L] is a concave function of task complexity relative to current competence–near-zero for tasks that are already solved under the current representation, near-zero for tasks that exceed the agent’s effective capacity/priors, and maximal near the boundary where errors are frequent but systematically reducible.

This dynamic generates an emergent curriculum without explicit programming. Because the physical world is compositionally structured (e.g., edges form shapes, shapes form objects, objects form scenes), the "learnable frontier" moves hierarchically. The agent initially focuses on simple sensorimotor primitives; once these are compressed (mastered), the marginal return on attending to them vanishes (phenomenologically experienced as boredom). This frees cognitive resources to attend to correlations between these now-compressed primitives, effectively "leveling up" the internal model to more abstract representations. The developmental progression from facial recognition -> object permanence -> chunked actions -> language -> abstract knowledge is therefore the trajectory of a locally-optimal learner whose reward landscape endogenously reshapes as skills saturate.

This yields a characteristic developmental dynamic:

Early: many domains offer large ΔL̂(π)\widehat{\Delta L}(\pi) →\to broad exploration and rapid acquisition of reusable primitives.

Middle: progress concentrates at the current frontier →\to sustained practice, skill chaining, and compositional growth (new goals formed from mastered subskills/options).

Late: as local progress saturates, the system restores learning progress by (i) switching domains/environments (novelty), or (ii) changing representational level (chunking, abstraction, new latent factors), enabling a new round of compression.

Importantly, this framework presupposes that agents can estimate expected compression gain 𝔼[ΔL|π]\mathbb{E}[\Delta L|\pi] for candidate policies. This metacognitive capacity itself requires a second-order model: a model of how the first-order world model changes under different experiences. Several mechanisms have been proposed:

1. Proxy signals: Using prediction error variance, gradient magnitude, or ensemble disagreement as heuristic estimators of ΔL\Delta L.

2. Memory-based extrapolation: Storing a history of (π,ΔL)(\pi,\Delta L) pairs and generalizing via function approximation.

3. Structural inference: Estimating task complexity from observable features (e.g., dimensionality, stationarity) and comparing against current model capacity.

Developmental evidence suggests this metacognitive capacity is itself learned–young children notoriously overestimate their competence in novel domains (poor calibration), while adults show systematic biases (e.g., the Dunning-Kruger effect).
